doc.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Teaching heads and Sweets Edison on the Basie band's head arrangements
summary: He has students learn heads and improvise backgrounds, recalling Sweets Edison saying the Basie band had no written book.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Do you memorize some heads with them?
Do you make them memorize melodies?

Um humm. In fact, we try to work more on heads rather than music. Some things we might use say a lead sheet. But if you notice blues bands, they’re very improvisational on the gig. You know you hear them come up with these backgrounds and things, you know like making up just on the spot. And this is what I’m trying to teach them to do and they love that. The first couple of weeks they’re kind of in the dark, then somebody will — as they used to say in the old days — set a riff, and they pick it up like that. And they’re all good musicians because well still as before, you have to audition to get into the school.

And you have to be a sophomore to get into my class. So they are pretty well trained on things like that by the time they get there. It works good. Because I tell them stories like Sweets Edison told me once that the Basie Band of the late ‘30s and early ‘40s did not have a book, they had no written music. And some of those early records you hear are head arrangements. I say are you serious? He says yeah. Somebody in a section will just like pay a riff and I guess their ears are so trained from playing jazz, jazz being improvisational I guess you must have good ears. And they would pick it up just like that, and you would think that all of this stuff was written out. But now it’s all written out you know, but back then, he says no.
